"TEAM" WORK
$18,980 FOR CHINESE

East night, the accounts were made up in connection with the annual membership and financial campaign of the Chinese Y.M.C.A. in the organisation of which various "teams" were formed.
The result exceeded anticipations, the directors having set themselves out to raise $12,000 whereas the sum actually found to be collected was $18,980.
One of the "teams," captained by Mr. Sun Chi-hing and Mr. Kwok Lam-fong, collected over $6,000.
HARBOUR MYSTERY.
No-one has been reported as missing locally and as the body was in an advanced state of decomposition the task of establishing identity is rendered even more difficult.
Mystery surrounds the identity of a deceased European whose body was recovered from the Harbour yesterday afternoon off Blackhead Point, near Holt's Wharf.
The body was clothed in light trousers, black serge jacket and blue and white striped shirt. There was no collar or necktie. The man also had on a pair of dark socks and black shoes.
THE MOSCOW STATE BALLET.

The Moscow State Ballet finished its season last night at the Queen's Theatre and will open to night at 9.15 at the Star Theatre, Kowloon. The programme is entirely new, not yet having been shown in Hong Kong. It consists of two big ballets, one Les Silphydes inspired by music of Chopin and the other is "A Holiday in a Russian Village," Folk dances etc. The programme is a very promising one. The opportunity is a unique one for Kowloon residents who have not yet seen this "wonderful" State Ballet.
SEAMENS MISSION

Though the whole year in the prospect is overshadowed by the disturbing events which occurred during the latter half, and we are inclined to think of 1925 almost entirely in the terms of "Strike and Boycott," we must not lose sight of the fact that the opening months appeared to present hopes of increase of trade and consequent general prosperity in the Colony. The disappointment of these hopes has thus seemed all the more dis

Early in March the Chaplain returned from home leave, and very soon afterwards the Rev. N. A. Peel who had been in charge for the time received orders to go to Bombay, paid a flying visit to Peking and finally sailed for India towards the end of April, leaving behind him in Hongkong the memory of a happy and charming personality.

It was not first intended that the work should be carried on by two chaplains, but the serious financial position of the Society locally made it unadvisable to arrange for another assistant chaplain to come out and also made it necessary to close down the Kowloon Institute, the running of which had proved a greater drain on the General Fund than "was originally" estimated. Thereafter the work for a month or two fell into the ordinary summer routine, when it was judely interrupted by the outbreak of trouble in June.

For a few days there seemed a distinct chance that the Institute Staff would remain unimpaired, but the receipt of one of the notorious "dagger" letters of intimidation brought out the servants on bloc, with the exception of three, the No. 1 and the No. 2 Boys, and the Manager's House Boy, who throughout all the trouble and afterwards did their full share of work in keeping things going.

The exposure of boys took place of a Sunday just ten minutes before evening service was due to begin As it was, there were no intending worshippers, " and the staff had a once to deal with the necessary changes in house routine. For the time it was decided that no boarders could be taken in except those already in residence, and all casual meals were ruled out. The boarders, where possible, took over the cleaning of their own cabins. Mrs. Sellwood, the Manager's wife, did the necessary marketing. The Manager's House Boy proved himself to be a really first rate cook, the other two boys looked after the ground floor of the building and the general service, while the rest of the Housework was taken on by the Chaplain, the Manager and his wife. The Chaplain and the Manager also had various duties to perform in connection with the defence and running of essential services in the Colony... All the boarders had meanwhile taken on jobs in various capacities as bakers, tramwyumen, in charge of tugs and lighters, etc., etc. At first it was necessary to have a European continually on duty in the entrance hall. During the first few days the work was various panicky alarms from some of our neighbours. " For instance care man-man in with a report of attempted a son and so on. All this naturally put a temporary start to the g" cater part of our usual work, more especially as the "Dayspring" was also laid up for lack of " a crew. It was particularly annoying in that from the Institute we could see day by day the great number of vessels lying in Kowloon. Buy waiting and mostly waiting in vain for their usual "runs" to be opened up again. It was fortunate that the launch coxgwin though at first intimidated "out" with the rest of the crew kept an eye on the launch and reported at the Institute after a couple of days, undertaking very necessary painting work in side the building until, after four weeks, the motor launch crews returned to work, and our activities in that respect were resumed.
It was however considerably

It was however considerably longer before we were able to get together a sufficient number of servants to enable us to open up the Institute to its full extent, though the utmost praise is due to the staff who did wonders in carrying on, at a time when they might justifiably have been content with doing the bare minimum to make life in the Institute possible.

So soon as the "Dayspring" was at work again we re-started the bathing picnics, though this was the only form of outdoor entertainment possible till late in the year, the tennis parties being out of the question, considering the fact that most if not all of our usual hostages were like ourselves running their households with no servants or a very greatly reduced staff. Entertaining under such

conditions was of course not to be expected.
In one respect, the trouble strangely enough brought us more indoor social work than is usually the case in the hot weather, for no sooner had H.M.S. "Hermes" with her aeroplanes arrived in port than arrangements for ship's company's dances were made and from about the middle of August to the end of the year there were as a general rule at least two dances a week in the Institute Hall as well as occasional Whist Drives. The Dance Club from the Flagship, H.M.S. "Haykins" also booked the Hall for regular weekly dances. We must pay grateful tribute to the willing spirit displayed by the organisers of these dances in falling in with our house rules and regulations. There were two or three carnival dances at one of which we were fortunate in having a large contingent from the crew of one of the big Tourist Ships, and just before Christmas, with the assistance of the Flagship, we entertained the ship's company of the French Flagship "Jules Michelet," at a dance, being honoured by the presence of Rear Admiral M. Basire, the French Consul, and several of the leading French residents in the Colony, as well as of course many of our British friends.

Our Christmas festivities took the form of a dinner followed by games in old fashioned style, and this party was quite an international affair, as we had men from British American and French ships. The ship's company of the "Jules Michele!" presented an old French Naval Engraving to the Institute as a token of appreciation, before their vessel left Hongkong.

We were delighted to welcome Lady Clementi at the Institute's room after her arrival in the Colony. Her interest in the welfare of the seafaring classes in Hongkong is well known, and as far as we are concerned her sympathy has taken the practical form of organising a Ladies' Entertainment Committee. In addition to the already existing Tennis Committee, for running periodical entertainments of various sorts in the Institute. The offer of the use of a tennis court at Government House was also very greatly appreciated, though circumstances so far have not enabled us to take advantage of this privilege.

It is not likely that the tennis parties as run formerly will be carried on in quite the same way until shipping and trade has resumed its more or less normal state, but we are sincerely grateful to Mrs. D. G. M. Bernard and other friends for their interest and help in arranging that the outdoor, social activities should not suffer more than necessary owing to the prevalent trouble. In the early part of the year of course tennis parties were held, and for the kindness in carrying those out we thank all those concerned.

Mention has already been made of our bathing parties, which were brought to a stop for two months, but were resumed as soon as practicable. Needless to say they proved as popular as ever. The "Daysspring," with the exception of the period specified, carried on her good work throughout the year in undiminished activity. Our thanks are due to all who in one way or another made it possible for us to keep her as clean and smart as such a vessel should be.

Owing to the presence in part of so many of H.M. Vessels for longer times than usual our indoor social figures show an increase, though those quoted only record attendances of seafarers at "shows" organised by us, and does not include ship's company dances which for the most part are run by the Ships' Dancing Clubs.

The loss sustained by the Society owing to the Strike and Boycott is shewn most clearly when we come to deal with statistics. The numbers of seafarers attending our Church Services were seriously affected, a misfortune if it can be called so, which we shared with the branch in Shanghai. In both "stations" for Sunday after Sunday, where previously the seafolk attendance had averaged about 25 or more according to the shipping in port, the numbers dropped to single figures. In spite of this, however, in Hongkong we are only some, 120 "down" on the 1924 figures, while we are thankful to be able to report that there is a slight increase in the number of attendances at Celebrations of the Holy Communion.

The beds occupied during the year also show a decrease, for it must be remembered that during part of the trouble men were not allowed to sleep ashore, but had to return on board each night, and also that for some little time, only those men who were already boarding in the Institute were able to sleep third owing to the greatly diminished staff being only able to cope with that much of the work.
When we come to deal with finance, we find there the most evident results of all the trouble. And in this we have cause for very careful and anxious thought.

The largest demonstration of women since the days of the Suffragettes was carried out under the auspices of the Women's Guild of Empire to-day, when 20,000 marched from the City to the Albert Hall to participate in an anti-strike meeting.

The gathering was composed of all classes of the community. A large proportion of the demonstrators reached the Metropolis in special trains and charabances from Scotland, Wales and the provinces. There was some display of unsympathetic feeling.

We started the year with an adverse Balance of over $11,500; and our aim was to clear at least some of this off during 1926 Circumstances unfortunately proved against us, and for the rest of the twelve months all we could hope to do was to keep the work going.

The Hongkong and Shanghai Banking Corporation were good enough to allow us to increase the mortgage on the Seamen's Institute from $60,000 to $90,000, covering not only the Reclamation Fund No. 2 Account, but also the overdraft on the Current Account, up to a limit of $15,000. This enabled us to carry on, but the end of December came with the limit nearly reached, and certain investments bringing in no interest. A further result of the boycott was the increase in unemployment most of those men so unfortunately situated being officers and engineers of the River Steamers, whose savings were soon exhausted. These men we could not possibly refuse to take in at the Institute, for the fault was not theirs, and at any time it seemed likely that their posts in the steamers would be open again, and though when able to do so, they will undoubtedly repay us any money owed us, this sad state of affairs has made it increasingly hard for us to make both ends meet. We always have certain bad debts mostly incurred by men who made vague promises to pay some time men whom we are here for the very purpose of helping and could help far more easily if they would only help themselves. If these debts could be repaid we should be in a much better position, but as it is we have had to limit the extent of our help to the most necessary and reasonable cases. Needless to say, it is most difficult to say "No," when perhaps another chance may make all the difference. The year finished financially with a debit balance of $15,278.31, bad debts amounting to $2,063.00.

The financial stress as already stated was one of the causes of the closing of the Kowloon Institute. At one time it seemed likely that we should be able to let the building and in fact all had been done but the signing of the papers, but it was discovered during an inspection of the structure that one of the walls had very recently developed signs of weakness, due it is believed to the thrust of the roof, and the cost of even the most necessary repairs alone was prohibitive considering the exhausted state of our exchequer. At the close of the year no definite decision had been made as to the future of the building.
We have received from many sources generous and willing assistance in trying to raise money. In April the Band of the 1st Battalion of the East Surrey Regiment, by kind permission of Lieut.-Colonel Montague Bates, C.B., D.S.O., gave a very successful orchestra concert on our behalf in the Theatre Royal, the Hongkong Jockey Club made a large donation, and St. Stephen's Girls' College sent a substantial sum as a part of the proceeds of a concert given by them in the School Hall. The Institute of Engineers and Ship builders of Hongkong again voted a substantial grant to us.

To one and all then we extend our grateful thanks for help given in so many different ways. We feel that though at present our position is straitened, yet so much sympathy has been shown us that we should be proving ourselves culpably lacking in faith and in belief in our great cause and above all in our Leader did we give way to despondency. We believe that the call has gone out that this work shall be done, and we believe that He Who has bidden us do it will give us the strength and the means and therefore that the period of stress through which we are now passing is merely a means to increase our faith and to make us more entirely dependent on Him Who said "According to your faith be it unto you." G. T. Waldegrave
CHINESE STUDE

Three main reasons why the Chinese students played so big a part in this country were suggested by Mr. Harry F. Kingman, in the course of a talk to members of the Tientsin Rotary Club at the weekly gathering at the Astor House recently. The first was the traditional respect and reverence of the Chinese for educated people. They had always looked to the scholarly for leadership, and here the educated classes enjoyed a prestige which students in other countries did not have. Secondly, the students of China were organised. Since May 80 they had developed an organisation capable of creating a national movement in three or four days. Thirdly, in China at present there was only a comparatively small group of people who understood national affairs and took an interest in them, and who were at the same time disinterested. Of that small group the students formed a considerable proportion. Many people felt that the students, no matter how many mistakes they made, were not trying to get something for themselves, and that although they sometimes used asining methods their ideal was right, and naturally that gave them a hearing with the common people.
Students Off the Right Road.

A good many people, especially in Shanghai, were interested in the students, because they could not help it. Some of them were anxious as to what was going to happen next month, when five anniversary days occurred. It was often felt that the students had gone off the right road during the past few months, and people were suspicious whenever the word "student" was mentioned. He (Mr. Kingman) deprecated the error of grouping people under one head, which seemed altogether too prevalent. Labour for instance, considered that "all capitalists were oppressors. In point of fact there were great differences among the student body. There were the same gradings as in other bodies, and even after May 30 moderates and radicals struggled for control of the movement, the former to give it a reasonable course and the other to force extreme measures. Chinese students had been accused of Bolshevik tendencies. That was true of some students. Many of them had been very favourable toward Russia, because the present Government of that country had been the first voluntarily to renounce their special privileges in his country, but since the action of the Soviet in connection with the Chinese Eastern Railway a tremendous revulsion of feeling bad developed. It would be a mistake to think that the students swallowed all that the Russians told them.

A Force To Be Reckoned With:
There was no doubt much truth in the assertion that the students were much impressed with their rights but far less concerned with their duties. "But with their weaknesses they had their strong points. Quite a large number of them were rather indifferent to national affairs. Sometimes, as when incidents like that of May 30 occurred, they were galvanised into activity. But as a rule they went on with their normal activities and paid small attention to national affairs. ESCORT WITH WIRELESS

Three United States army planes, equipped with wireless, left Camp Nichols on April 26 for Aparri, where they will await the arrival of Captains Loriga and Galianza, the Spanish Madrid-to-Manila fliers, (says the "Manila Bulletin.")

The planes are of the latest type in use by the aviation corps in the Philippines. They are piloted by First Lt. Paul L. Williams, Corregidor, First Lt. Stanley M. Umstead, Corregidor, and First Lt. Harry M. Mills, Camp Stotsenburg.

The three American filers will escort the Spanish airmen from Aparri to Camp Nichols. The American and Spanish filers will come down over the Cagayan Valley, Isabela province, Bayombong, Nueva Vizcaya province; Balete Pass, Nueva Vizcaya province; San Jose, Nueva Vizcaya province, and Camp Stotsenburg, Pampanga. It is understood that twelve places from Camp Stotsenburg will accompany the filers from there to Camp Nichols.
The arrival of Captains Loriga and Gallarza in Manila is indefinite.

Usually they tried to use moderate measures, and consulted their faculties and other foreigners whom they deemed to be sympathetic. They had done a great deal for their country in the past. One might go back 2,000 years and find them going out to help their country. Usually they got it "in the neck," though not perhaps as in Peking a month ago. But in the long run, what they did created public opinion. They were a force to be reckoned with, and would do things in the future. If foreigners took a more sympathetic attitude toward them it would keep the more conservative group to gain the mastery and to take control out of the hands of the radicals.

Rotarian Harvey, in tendering the Club's thanks to Mr. Klingman for his address, said he had always contended that students should find no place in active politics. His business gave him considerable knowledge of educational institutions in this country, and he generally found that in well organised Mission schools and private institutions there was very little trouble. Most of the trouble emanated from the national Colleges, where there was usually corruption from the head downward. One reason for discontent was the lack of opportunity for those who were completing their studies. However, there were no students in the world he admired more highly than, for instance, those of Nankai and of the Hui Wen Middle School in Tientsin. They had great difficulties in getting an efficient education, because owing to the absence of native text books they had to acquire their education through an acquired language. In such institutions the students were found at work from early morning till late at night. They were a most industrious lot and he respected every one of them.
FAR EAST RADIO
SHANGHAI SERVICE TO MANILA.
START THIS MONTH?

Successful short wave tests recently have been conducted by the Far Eastern Radio Corporation between the local station and newly-erected station in Shanghai, according to B. Razon, the Shanghai manager of the corporation.

sible that the new radio service would be opened for commercial dispatches next month. He was slightly pessimistic, however, owing to some irregularities which still have to be straightened out before the Shanghai station can commence operation.

"Radio materials are considered contraband of war in China," said Mr. Razon, "and difficulty is being experienced in attempting to learn from whom it is necessary to secure authority to operate our Shanghai station. However, steps are being taken to secure the necessary authority, and it is possible that a commercial service between Shanghai and Manila will be established by next month."

Mr. Razor also said that the station in Seattle was nearing completion and that he expected the Far Eastern Radio Corporation would establish commercial service between Manila and Seattle within the next three or four months.

Owing to the rapidity of transmission and the low cost of sending messages by the short wave route Mr. Razon believes that once in operation, the commercial service of the Far Eastern Radio Corporation between Manila, Shanghai and Seattle will be greatly in demand. "Manila Bulletin."
